tldr: A new method that significantly boosts 3D drone navigation accuracy and safety by first "imagining" local visual features of the next destination as a linear combination of prototype representations before predicting actions.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of ProtoVis-Nav. Taking dual-view RGB images, language instructions, and drone states as inputs, it adds LoRA adapters and dedicated special tokens (<stop>, <pvi>, and <wp>) to a frozen Qwen3VL backbone to perform visual imagination and trajectory generation simultaneously.
overview:
Vision-Language Navigation (VLN), where an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) follows natural language instructions through 3D space, is far more challenging than ground robot navigation. Small 3D motion prediction errors quickly lead to navigation failures and fatal collisions. Most existing methods regress waypoints directly from images and instructions. However, lacking an understanding of execution outcomes—what scene will appear next after taking an action—makes safe trajectory planning difficult.

Recently, approaches using world models to generate full future video frames or latent states have emerged. Yet, they are computationally prohibitive for precise drone flight. Furthermore, predicting full-scene backgrounds does not directly help with fine-grained decisions like slipping through narrow gaps. The authors thus focused on a key intuition: instead of generating entire future scenes, is it sufficient to pinpoint and imagine only the local region the drone intends to reach next?

This paper introduces ProtoVis-Nav. It re-projects the next target position onto the current camera image and uses the feature representation of that local patch as ground truth. The model is forced to predict these visual features in advance via a linear combination of prototype tokens (<pvi>), and then uses this latent representation as context to predict the next waypoint (<wp>). Evaluations on benchmarks such as OpenUAV and HUGE-Bench show that ProtoVis-Nav substantially outperforms existing baselines in success rates while drastically reducing collision risks.
contributions: Proposed an efficient, direct visual imagination task focusing on a local patch re-projected from the next target location onto the current image, rather than predicting full-frame future scenes.

Developed a PVI head that estimates local patch features via a linear combination of prototype tokens instead of directly regressing them with an MLP, preventing overfitting and providing context for waypoint prediction.

Introduced a dynamic view selection mechanism that automatically identifies horizontal vs. vertical motions (takeoff, landing, rapid climb/descent) to decide whether to crop target patches from the front or downward camera.
Demonstrated navigation success rates and obstacle avoidance performance significantly outperforming existing VLM-based and foundation model baselines on OpenUAV and HUGE-Bench.

sections.heading: Challenges in Drone Navigation and the Idea of Local Imagination
sections.summary: In language-guided navigation for drones flying in 3D space, tiny motion errors directly cause collisions. To overcome the limits of simple waypoint regression and heavy full-frame video world models, the authors propose pinpointing and imagining only the local region of the next movement target.
sections.details:
In Embodied AI, Vision-Language Navigation (VLN)—navigating environments by following language instructions—is an active research area. Originally focused on ground robots moving in flat, structured indoor environments, research has recently expanded to UAVs flying freely in 3D space. However, drones have higher degrees of freedom, requiring advanced 3D spatial awareness and precise motion control.

The biggest problem when applying existing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) is that models regress continuous waypoints directly from images and language without considering execution outcomes—what the scene will look like as a result of their actions. Because the training loss only accounts for geometric waypoint errors, models cannot evaluate action safety in advance and tend to generate dangerous trajectories.

In contrast, "world model" approaches using video generation models to predict full future observations have emerged. However, what really matters in drone flight is not background transitions, but tiny local areas like a narrow gap to pass through. Full-scene video generation is impractical due to high computational overhead and uncertainty.

Therefore, this paper proposes ProtoVis-Nav (Prototypical Visual Imagination). It projects the future target location onto the current camera plane and predicts the feature representation of the local patch around it. Furthermore, rather than simply regressing features, it expresses them as a linear combination of multiple prototype tokens, providing a compact, regularized visual context for subsequent action prediction.

sections.heading: From Ground to Air, and From Global World Models to Local Imagination
sections.summary: This section reviews the evolution of UAV VLN research and world models that incorporate future prediction. The proposed method carves out a distinct position by moving away from computationally heavy global scene generation to focus specifically on local visual evidence at movement targets.
sections.details:
Related work falls into two main categories.

### Language-Guided Navigation for UAVs (UAV VLN)
VLN started with ground robots and was extended to drones through studies like TravelUAV, NavFoM, LongFly, and OpenVLN. TravelUAV regresses waypoints directly from observations and kinematics, while NavFoM explored a cross-embodiment foundation model trained on large-scale data. LongFly structures redundant temporal histories compactly, and OpenVLN optimizes VLMs using reinforcement learning. However, all these methods rely on past history or current geometry, lacking a mechanism to actively consider future local visual cues—what the upcoming destination visually looks like.

### Navigation World Models
World models giving agents future-prediction capabilities are actively studied. Pathdreamer and Dreamwalker generate panoramic images or environment graphs, and NWM simulates future video trajectories using a Diffusion Transformer. More compact methods predicting future states in latent space, such as UNeMo, MonoDream, and DriveVLA-W0, have also been proposed.

However, existing world models focus on generating whole scenes or panoramic views. Safe drone navigation requires local visual evidence, such as obstacles or gaps around the next target location, rather than a coarse global view. ProtoVis-Nav clearly sets itself apart from global world models—and from prior work like ReconVLA that reconstructs focus regions for manipulation—by projecting the next target point onto the current frame and predicting local patch features using prototypes.

sections.heading: Core Method: Teaching Where to Look and What to Imagine
sections.summary: Built on Qwen3VL, this system integrates three special tokens: stopping (<stop>), visual imagination (<pvi>), and waypoint prediction (<wp>). It selects camera views based on horizontal and vertical motion characteristics, projects future targets onto the current image, and reconstructs visual features via prototypes.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Overall Pipeline
The model adopts Qwen3VL-2B-Instruct as its backbone. Inputs consist of front and downward dual-view RGB images (each $256\times 256$), natural language instructions, and drone state quantities (such as previous-step displacements and current positions). The backbone weights are frozen, and only LoRA adapters and additional output heads are trained.

Three special query tokens are introduced into the input:
- `<stop>`: Determines whether the episode should terminate.
- `<pvi>`: Generates visual prototypes for the next local target region ($K$ tokens placed).
- `<wp>`: Predicts waypoints, referencing the latent representations of preceding `<pvi>` tokens as context.

### 3.2 Visual Imagination Target Formulation
During training, drone positions at the current step $t$ and next step $t+1$ ($\bm{p}_t, \bm{p}_{t+1}$) are obtained from expert trajectories. Predicting the full future image $\bm{x}_{t+1}$ is too difficult, so this method sets "where to head in the current image $\bm{x}_t$" as the training target. Specifically, the next target position $\bm{p}_{t+1}$ is projected onto the current camera plane to obtain coordinates $\bm{p}_{\text{proj}}$, and a $32\times 32$ pixel patch $\tilde{\bm{x}}$ around it is cropped.

The choice between the front and downward cameras matters because drones execute vertical climbs, descents, takeoffs, and landings in addition to forward flight. When altitude change within a short window satisfies $|\Delta z| > 5\text{ m}$ or the vertical-to-horizontal motion ratio $\rho > 0.8$, motion is deemed vertical-dominant and the downward image is chosen; otherwise, motion is horizontal-dominant and the front image is selected.

### 3.3 Prototypical Visual Imagination Head (PVI Head)
The cropped local patch feature $\tilde{\bm{v}}$ is extracted by the Qwen3-VL vision encoder (producing $N=1$ token for a $32\times 32$ patch). Rather than directly regressing this feature via an MLP, the PVI head predicts it as a linear combination of hidden states $\bm{h}_k$ from the $K=16$ `<pvi>` tokens. Using mixing weights $\alpha_k$ obtained via Softmax over a learnable projection, it computes $\hat{\bm{v}} = \sum_{k=1}^K \alpha_k \bm{h}_k$ and optimizes it against $\tilde{\bm{v}}$ using Smooth L1 and cosine similarity losses. Using prototypes as basis vectors prevents overfitting while enabling the subsequent `<wp>` token to attend to high-quality visual context directly tied to action decisions.

captions.F2: Process of selecting imagination target regions during training. On the left, camera views (front vs. downward) are selected based on horizontal-vertical motion ratios. On the right, the next target point is projected onto the current image to crop a $32\times 32$ local patch.
captions.F3: Architecture of the Prototypical Visual Imagination Head. Hidden states of $K$ <pvi> tokens are linearly combined using Softmax-normalized weights and trained to match target patch features extracted by the image encoder.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Higher Success Rates and Better Safety
sections.summary: Evaluations on OpenUAV and HUGE-Bench show consistent gains over baselines across all tasks, including unseen environments (Test Unseen). Detailed ablations demonstrate the superiority of local imagination over global prediction and the necessity of the prototype design.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluations were conducted on the physics-based simulation environment OpenUAV (on the TRAVEL platform) and HUGE-Bench (an obstacle-avoidance region transit task combining 3D Gaussian Splatting and meshes).
Key evaluation metrics include Navigation Error (NE, final distance to goal, lower is better), Success Rate (SR), Oracle Success Rate (OSR, reaching the goal at least once along the path), and Success weighted by Path Length (SPL). HUGE-Bench also evaluates Collision Rate (CR) and collision-weighted CSPL.

### 4.2 Performance Comparison
In OpenUAV's seen environment (Test Seen Full), ProtoVis-Nav achieved NE of 51.77 m, SR of 50.78%, and SPL of 44.68%, outperforming all strong baselines including TravelUAV, NavFoM, and LongFly. Compared to its own base model without the imagination mechanism (Base), SR improved from 46.47% to 50.78% and NE dropped from 55.67 m to 51.77 m. In unseen environments (Test Unseen Full), it achieved top scores of 30.12% SR and 27.53% SPL, showing strong generalization.
In HUGE-Bench obstacle avoidance tasks (averaged over 5 runs), SR jumped from 36.39% to 47.47% over Base, while Collision Rate (CR) dropped substantially from 54.46% to 39.76%.

### 4.3 Safety Analysis
In OpenUAV collision analysis, ProtoVis-Nav reduced CR from 36.44% to 34.41% compared to Base, expanding the mean clearance to obstacles from 16.72 m to 16.82 m. Near-miss rates within 0.5 m, 1.0 m, and 1.5 m of obstacles consistently decreased, confirming fewer hazardous flights.

### 4.4 Variant Studies (Ablations)
- **Imagination Target Selection**: Comparing front-view only, center crop, and future full frame, the proposed "current image projection patch" performed best. Fixed center cropping degraded NE to 69.06 m, highlighting the importance of projecting target locations to crop local areas.
- **PVI Head Design**: Directly regressing target features using an MLP instead of a linear combination of prototypes hurt all metrics. This confirms the benefit of storing visual features across prototype tokens as distributed representations for `<wp>` to read, rather than simply fitting features with a high-capacity MLP.
- **Number of Tokens $K$**: Testing $K \in \{4, 8, 16, 32\}$ showed that $K=16$ was optimal. Too few tokens lack representational capacity, while too many scatter information and introduce redundancy into `<wp>` context.

### 4.5 Visualizations and Attention Analysis
Visualizing spatial attention revealed that attention peaks for PVI tokens cleanly concentrated around projected target regions in the current image during both cruising and landing. Furthermore, causal attention matrices showed that `<wp>` tokens strongly attended to `<pvi>` tokens, confirming that waypoints are decided using the imagined visual context.

captions.F5: Ablation results across different numbers of PVI tokens $K$. At $K=16$, NE (black curve) is lowest, while SR (blue curve) and SPL (red curve) reach their peaks.
captions.F7: PVI spatial attention (left) and causal attention across tokens (right). PVI tokens attend to destination regions, while waypoint tokens (<wp>) strongly depend on PVI tokens.
captions.F8: Qualitative navigation example on OpenUAV. In a complex environment with street trees and buildings, the drone safely approaches and stops at the target white truck while handling viewpoint shifts.

sections.heading: Implementation Details and Extra Validation: Trajectory Completion, Robustness, and Inference Interventions
sections.summary: This section covers distance-dependent soft labels for stopping, details on the Trajectory Completion Module that turns coarse waypoints into smooth 5-step trajectories, robustness against various noises, and inference intervention experiments masking or shuffling PVI tokens.
sections.details:
### A. Implementation Details (Stop Head and Trajectory Completion Module)
- **Stop Head Training**: Trained via binary cross-entropy with a distance-dependent soft label $y_{\text{stop}} = 1 / (1 + \exp(0.2(d - 20)))$ based on goal distance $d$. Probability is 0.5 at 20 m and approaches 1 closer to the goal. At inference, a stop command is issued when probability exceeds $\tau_{\text{stop}}=0.5$.
- **Trajectory Completion Module**: Instead of directly executing the coarse 3D waypoint $\bm{w}_{\text{llm}}$ from `<wp>`, this module concatenates it with current front image features and passes it through an MLP to refine it into a smooth, executable short-horizon trajectory (5 steps during inference). It functions as a local visual corrector without reading VLM language prompts.

### B & C. PVI Spatial Consistency and Feature Retrieval
Estimating target positions from similarity maps between predicted PVI features and image patch features, the proportion falling within 32 pixels of the true projected patch center reached 87.20% in Seen and 88.40% in Unseen environments. When retrieving the true patch among 841 candidate patches sampled densely across the image via cosine similarity, Recall@10 reached 80.40% in Seen and 69.30% in Unseen, confirming accurate visual feature reconstruction.

### D & F. Robustness and Backbone Comparisons
Under three perturbations—image noise, odometry noise, and actuator execution error—odometry noise harmed SR the most (dropping to 46.42%), while execution error degraded NE most (increasing to 59.92 m). Robustness to image noise was comparatively high.
Comparing backbones against a diffusion-based world-action model (Wan2.1-VACE), ProtoVis-Nav with Qwen3-VL reduced latency from 333.83 ms to 185.48 ms while boosting SR from 17.25% to 50.78%. Single-pass local feature imagination proved far more practical than multi-step full-frame generation.

### G. Inference-Time PVI Intervention Experiments
Manipulating PVI token outputs at inference showed that while intact SR was 50.78%, swapping PVI tokens with another sample (Shuffled) dropped SR to 41.09%, masking attention (Masked) dropped it to 37.87%, and replacing them with random values (Random) caused it to plummet to 36.75%. This decisively proves that `<wp>` tokens actively rely on grounded local visual information from PVI during inference, rather than treating it merely as training regularization.

captions.F9: Architecture of the Trajectory Completion Module detailed in Appendix A.3. It integrates coarse waypoints predicted by the VLM with current-frame front RGB features to produce smooth short-range local trajectories executable in AirSim.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook
sections.summary: ProtoVis-Nav is an innovative framework that improves visual-spatial alignment for action decisions by imagining local target visual features through prototype combinations. Extensive experiments confirm higher navigation accuracy and reduced collisions in continuous UAV navigation.
sections.details:
### Conclusion
This work highlights the importance of anticipating action outcomes in language-instructed UAV navigation. By discarding unrealistic full-scene future video generation in favor of projecting next movement targets onto current images and predicting local patch features, it offers a simple yet highly effective formulation.
Passing visual imagination results through prototype-based PVI tokens provides natural context to the waypoint prediction head, achieving tight visual-spatial alignment.

### Limitations and Future Work
The authors candidly acknowledge that collisions with thin, semi-transparent, or visually ambiguous obstacles—such as utility poles, thin tree branches, and power lines—remain the primary failure mode. Estimating safety margins for such fine obstacles from monocular RGB images alone is inherently difficult.
Future work points toward integrating LiDAR or depth sensors, incorporating explicit collision risk evaluation modules, and validating performance on physical hardware-in-the-loop setups beyond simulation.

takeaways: A world model does not need to generate full-screen video; imagining only the local target region directly tied to the task offers massive advantages in both efficiency and accuracy.

Predicting imagination features via a linear combination of prototype tokens—rather than regressing them directly with an MLP—enables passing useful context straight to subsequent action tokens (<wp>).
For 3D systems like drones where camera importance changes dramatically between forward flight and vertical movement, dynamic camera view selection tailored to motion characteristics is essential.
limitations: Restricted to RGB camera inputs, making it difficult to detect and avoid thin, subtle obstacles like power lines, thin branches, and streetlight poles, which account for the vast majority of failure cases.
Evaluations are limited to high-fidelity simulators like AirSim (OpenUAV, HUGE-Bench), lacking real-world physical drone experiments under wind disturbances and sensor noise.
